items.title: Percent and change
items.content: Percent means per hundred: \(p\%=p/100\). Part = rate × whole; percentage change \(=\frac{\text{change}}{\text{original}}\times100\%\). Successive percentage changes use the updated base.

items.title: Divisibility rules
items.content: 2: last digit even; 3/9: digit sum divisible by 3/9; 5: last digit 0 or 5; 10: last digit 0; 4: last two digits divisible by 4; 8: last three digits divisible by 8; 11: alternating digit-sum difference divisible by 11.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Write the base quantity beside every percentage calculation.
For an inverse discount question, divide by the remaining percentage factor.

items.title: Convert among percent, fraction and decimal
items.content: Worked example: \(37.5\%=0.375=3/8\). Divide a percent by 100 to get a decimal.

items.title: Find a percentage of a quantity
items.content: Worked example: 18% of 250 is \(0.18\times250=45\).

items.title: Find the whole or rate
items.content: Worked example: 30 is 12% of a number \(N\); \(0.12N=30\), so \(N=250\).

items.title: Percentage increase and decrease
items.content: Worked example: price rises from ₹800 to ₹920. Change is ₹120; increase is \(120/800\times100=15\%\).

items.title: Successive changes
items.content: Worked example: ₹1,000 rises by 10%, then falls by 10%: \(1000(1.1)(0.9)=₹990\), a net 1% decrease.

items.title: Divisibility rules in use
items.content: Worked example: 5,742 has digit sum 18, so it is divisible by 3 and 9; last two digits 42 are not divisible by 4.

items.title: Find a part, whole, or rate
items.content: Identify the base (whole). Worked example: 24% of 350 = \(0.24\cdot350=84\).

items.title: Percentage change
items.content: Use the original quantity as denominator. Worked example: a value falls from 80 to 68; decrease is \(12/80\times100=15\%\).

items.title: Reverse percentage
items.content: If ₹540 is after a 10% discount, it is 90% of marked price; marked price is \(540/0.9=₹600\). Worked example: ₹540 after a 10% discount is 90% of the marked price, so MP = 540/0.9 = ₹600.

items.title: Successive discounts or changes
items.content: Multiply factors such as \(1+r/100\) for increase and \(1-r/100\) for decrease. Worked example: +10% then −10% multiplies by 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99, a net 1% decrease.

items.title: Apply divisibility tests
items.content: Use last digits for powers of 2/5 and digit sums for 3/9; for 11 compare alternating sums. Worked example: 1,331 has alternating digit-sum difference 1 − 3 + 3 − 1 = 0, so it is divisible by 11.

items.title: Derive percentage formula
items.content: Since percent means “per hundred,” \(p\%\) of \(N\) is \(pN/100\). Rearranging gives percentage \(=100(\text{part}/\text{whole})\%\).

items.title: Why successive percentages do not add directly
items.content: Each percentage is applied to a different base. An increase by \(a\%\) and decrease by \(b\%\) multiply the original by \((1+a/100)(1-b/100)\).

items.title: Divisibility by 4 and 8
items.content: A number is \(100q+r\); since 100 is divisible by 4, divisibility by 4 depends on the last two digits. Since 1000 is divisible by 8, divisibility by 8 depends on the last three digits.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Wrong base for percentage change
items.content: Divide by the original value, not the new value.

items.title: Adding successive rates
items.content: Compose their multipliers; do not simply add an increase and decrease.

items.title: Percent versus percentage points
items.content: A change from 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points and a 25% relative increase.

items.title: Using one divisibility test for another
items.content: Check the exact rule and digit window for each divisor.

keyTakeaways: Percent is a ratio out of 100.
Percentage change uses the original value as its base.
Divisibility rules depend on place value and digit sums.
